pr_title: Gracefully stop host if hosted service stops the application during startup
pr_body:
This PR closes #51613 by introducing the following behavior when starting `IHostedService` from the `Host`:

1. Before starting each hosted service, check  `IHostApplicationLifetime` to see if the application has been instructed to stop and if so abort the start sequence.
2. If the application is not instructed to stop, check the provided `CancellationToken` to see if the caller has requested cancellation and if so throws `OperationCanceledException`.

Issue Details
This PR closes #51613 by introducing the following behavior when starting `IHostedService` from the `Host`: 1. Before starting each hosted service, check `IHostApplicationLifetime` to see if the application has been instructed to stop and if so abort the start sequence and begin stopping the application. If this happens, the application only stop the hosted services that has been started. The stopping of the application still respects the provided `CancellationToken` as well as the configured shutdown timeout. 2. If the application is not instructed to stop, check the provided `CancellationToken` to see if the caller has requested cancellation and if so throws `OperationCanceledException`.

reviewers, looks like this is pending action on our side cc @davidfowl @eerhardt @maryamariyan

@pardahlman - I'm still not convinced this is the correct behavior. Stopping a Host while it is in the middle of starting is similar to cancelling an operation. When we cancel an operation that is running, we throw an exception to signify that the operation hasn't been completed successfully. I think we should be doing the same here - throw an exception from `Start`, if the Host has been stopped while it was starting.

If an application wants to allow for stopping during start, it can catch the exception - just like it can catch an `OperationCanceledException`.

issue_context.title: Hosted services are started even though the application is instructed to stop.
issue_context.body:
### Description

As `Microsoft.Extensions.Hosting.Internal.Host` starts, it resolves all registered instances of  `IHostedService` and starts them in sequence. If a hosted service stops the application (using `IHostApplicationLifetime.StopApplication()`), the remaining hosted services are still started (that is `StartAsync` is called), despite the fact that the application is instructed to shut down.

This can results in a combination of the following behaviors:

* If any of the remaining hosted services checks the provided cancellation token and throws an exception, it propagates and results in an unhandled exception unless the user wraps the start call in try/catch. This feels unexpected, as the stopping should be considered graceful.
* If the remaining hosted services does not check the cancellation token, time and resources may be spent starting components that will just be stopped shortly after. This does not scale well if there are "a lot" of registered hosted services that takes "long" time to start.
 
I think it would make sense to check the `IHostApplicationLifetime.ApplicationStopping` cancellation token after each started hosted service and if it is triggered, gracefully exit the application.

One could also argue that `ThrowIfCancellationRequested` should be called on the cancellation token passed to `StartAsync`  after each started service.

Looking forward hearing your thoughts on this!

What's a the scenario for gracefully shutting down in start?

Hi @davidfowl , thanks for getting back on this issue this quickly 🙏 I suspect you're not going to be enthusiastic over the reasons behind why we want to do this, but here I go...

Basically, we are calling an external API that connects to a message broker and sets up consumers and producers for it. This call may fail for a number of reasons and if so it throws an exception. We want to log that exception and then shut down the application with a non-zero exit code. Sounds like an we should just throw an exception and let it be unhandled, right? We tried that, but something (which I now suspect is the runtime?) logs unhandled exception to the console. Everything that is written to stdout is ingested to one of our log system, so the exception was logged by our code and whatever it is that writes to the console. It would not do to just rely on the "logging" written to the console, as it does not follow our JSON schema for log entries, but more importantly, we have other logging providers that pushes data to other destinations.

We considered wrappng the call to `IHost.RunAsync` in a try/catch, but at this point we have too many services in too many repositories for such change to be feasible. Based on this I think you can guess what solution we ended up with: using `StopApplication` on `IHostApplicationLifetime`.

So that is the backstory... but, if we raise the issue to a more theoretical level, wouldn't you expect the scenario described in the issue to result in a graceful shutdown?

So if I got this right, you don't want the exception to be printed to the console, *and* you don't want to add a try/catch to your code, but you want a non-zero exit code for a graceful shutdown? 

The graceful shutdown sounds reasonable, but not the non-zero exit code.

You got it right 👌 The non-zero exit code is part of another implementation detail that has to do with compatibility with services still running on Windows. It has very little bearing for this issue. What I'm suggesting is that it would be reasonable to expect the following:

1. If an `IHostedService` stops the application (`IHostApplicationLifetime.StopApplication()`) it should result in a graceful shutdown, preferably as soon as possible (e.g. check before starting each `IHostedService`).
2. If cancellation is requested for the user provided `CancellationToken` it should throw an `OperationCanceledException` as soon as possible (e.g. check before starting each `IHostedService`)

If you think this makes sense I could submit an MR for these changes.

> If an IHostedService stops the application (IHostApplicationLifetime.StopApplication()) it should result in a graceful shutdown, preferably as soon as possible (e.g. check before starting each IHostedService).

This sounds reasonable. In this case is an exception thrown? If yes, how does it fix your scenario?

> If cancellation is requested for the user provided CancellationToken it should throw an OperationCanceledException as soon as possible (e.g. check before starting each IHostedService)

Yes this is fine.

> In this case is an exception thrown? If yes, how does it fix your scenario?

No, I would suggest that the graceful shutdown does not throw an unhandled exception, but instead aborts the starting up of hosted services, probably do some cleanup (like stopping the already started services? call `ApplicationLifetime.NotifyStopped`?) and then return.

I guess there is an argument that stopping the application (`IHostApplicationLifetime.StopApplication()`) triggers a cancellation request on the `CancellationToken` `ApplicationStopping`, which would be a reason to throw `OperationCanceledException`.  I haven't considered that to be a desired behavior, as I don't think an unhandled exception from `IHost.StartAsync` is graceful. Let me know if you're seeing this differently!

I've been giving this issue some more thought and created an PR with a suggestion of how to modify the startup behavior to respect `IHostApplicationLifetime.ApplicationStopping` and the user provided `CancellationToken` while starting up the hosted services. Looking forward hearing your thought on this!

> It would not do to just rely on the "logging" written to the console, as it does not follow our JSON schema for log entries

not completely related to the gist of this issue, but also wanted to mention that console logs can be written in a JSON format too when you use AddJsonConsole.

2. Another that uses IHostApplicationLifetime.StopApplication inside of an IHostedService.StartAsync (that's the scenario you were testing right?)

Thank you for this! 

1. If I understand you correctly and read the code right, you are asking for a test [for this existing line of code](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/025e7f60cb355f9c44a5ff20784118e785891a4c/src/libraries/Microsoft.Extensions.Hosting/src/Internal/Host.cs#L59) with `_applicationLifetime.ApplicationStopping` being cancelled? Or are you thinking in the lines of calling `IHostApplicationLifetime.StopApplication` as the hosted services [are being resolved from DI](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/025e7f60cb355f9c44a5ff20784118e785891a4c/src/libraries/Microsoft.Extensions.Hosting/src/Internal/Host.cs#L60)?
2. I believe that this scenario is covered in `HostStopsGracefullyIfHostedServiceStopsTheApplication`, where the first hosted service [calls StopApplication](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/52517/files#diff-0004f2f896ea10dbe221c137338cf0bf30e116223a38d91911966c58b4d5b5beR673). Let me know if there is something I missed here!

Can't we handle both cancellation token checks here with one line?

```C#
combinedCancellationToken.ThrowIfCancellationRequested();
```

Note that `combinedCancellationToken` is a combination of the `cancellationToken` parameter and `_applicationLifetime.ApplicationStopping`.

Thank you for this feedback 👍 The reasoning for this implementation is to get consistent behavior for calls to `IHostApplicationLifetime.StopApplication()`, despite the state of the host. I would argue that it is expected to get a graceful stop even though the call is made before the host is fully started.

However, I think that if the user provided `CancellationToken` is cancelled, it should throw, since this is expected behavior from other APIs that accept a `CancellationToken`.

So to sum it up: before starting each hosted service, check if the application is instructed to stop, if so, return from the Start method and let the host begin continue to stop. Next, check if the user has requested cancellation, and if so throw exception.

Looking forward hearing your thoughts on this!

Did you see @davidfowl's comments here?

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/52517#discussion_r629436543

> It's weird to return from StartAsync without an error if we haven't successfully started.
Maybe it's fine but I haven't thought enough about the implications. Is there anything that would be broken if the started event didn't fire but StartAsync returns successfully?
